game-boy.history: When Nintendo launched the Game Boy in 1989, few suspected that a pocket console with a greenish monochrome display would outlive its technically more advanced rivals by years. The machine was designed by **Gunpei Yokoi** according to his famous philosophy of "lateral thinking with seasoned technology" — instead of the newest and most expensive components, he bet on cheap, proven and reliable ones. The result was paradoxically perfect: together with the later Game Boy Color, over **118 million units** were sold, making the Game Boy the most successful handheld of its era. The secret of its success was threefold. Battery life — the Game Boy ran on four AA cells for a comfortable fifteen hours or more, while the color competition in the form of the Atari Lynx or Sega Game Gear devoured them in a few hours. Low price. And above all software: the bundled **Tetris** was so addictive that it sold the console on its own, and a few years later came **Pokémon**, which breathed a second life into the Game Boy at a time when it was already technically long outdated. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the Game Boy is the **8-bit Sharp LR35902 processor**, a hybrid between the Intel 8080 and the Zilog Z80, clocked at around 4.19 MHz. The display shows a resolution of **160 × 144 pixels** and only **four shades** — although people speak of "grays", in reality these were various levels of green given by the type of LCD used. The original model had no backlight at all, so to play you needed decent ambient light (or the famous add-on lamp). The graphics hardware handled hardware **sprites** (up to 40 at once, max. 10 per line) and smooth background scrolling, which made the Game Boy a solid platform for platformers and action games. On the sound side it offered **four channels**: two pulse channels (square wave) with frequency sweep, one wave channel with a programmable table and one noise channel for drums and effects. It was precisely this modest sound set that gave rise to the unmistakable **chiptune** sound, which today lives a life of its own in modern electronic music. ### Connectivity and peripherals On the side of the console you find the **Link cable** — a connection of two Game Boys via a serial port. This enabled not only multiplayer (the legendary Tetris duels) but also the trading of Pokémon, without which a collection could not be completed. There was also a four-player adapter for selected titles. The peripherals included the **Game Boy Camera** (one of the first affordable digital cameras for consumers) and the **Game Boy Printer** for thermal paper. There was also rumble and tilt sensors built directly into some cartridges (e.g. Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble). Saving positions was handled by a battery right inside the game module, which powered the SRAM memory — which is why on old cartridges the saves disappear today once the button battery dies. ### Models and revisions The original **DMG-01** from 1989 was brick-like and large. In 1996 came the significantly smaller and lighter **Game Boy Pocket** with a sharper black-and-white display (and one button battery instead of the four AA cells). Shortly thereafter followed the **Game Boy Light** — for the Japanese market only, with a backlit display. The breakthrough model was the **Game Boy Color** (1998): it kept backward compatibility with old games, but added a color display and a faster processor. The line was completed by the **Game Boy Advance** (2001) with a 32-bit core, which could also run the original GB and GBC titles — the era of the eight-bit handheld console thus smoothly transitioned into a new generation. ### Clones and variants The Game Boy was not as massively cloned as the NES, but unofficial copies existed — all sorts of imitations circulated in Asia, along with pirated multicart modules with hundreds of games on a single chip. In the Eastern Bloc and in China, cheap "pocket game" handhelds appeared that imitated the shape and controls of the Game Boy, even though inside they ran on completely different (and weaker) hardware. For Czech and Slovak players it is fair to add that the legal route to Nintendo was practically closed before 1989 — which is why clones of home computers spread among us more than the Game Boy (the Didaktik as the Czechoslovak relative of the ZX Spectrum) and later famiclones of the Pegasus type for the eight-bit NES. The Game Boy reached us mainly through imports only in the 1990s. ### Today's scene Emulation of the Game Boy is trivial today — it runs on practically anything, from a phone to cheap retro handhelds. Among the top emulators are **mGBA** and **SameBoy**, which faithfully imitates even the characteristic motion "blur" of the original LCD. The homebrew community is surprisingly lively. Technically advanced new releases are being created, such as the brisk **Tobu Tobu Girl** or the atmospheric horror **Deadeus**, the creation of chiptune music flourishes (the **LSDj** software) and thanks to the **GB Studio** tool even a person without programming knowledge can put together their own game for the Game Boy today. Some of those new releases boldly measure up to the period classics.

game-boy-color.history: When the Game Boy Color arrived in 1998, Nintendo was not dealing with a revolution — it was dealing with maintaining the throne. The original Game Boy from 1989 and its interim step, the Game Boy Pocket, were still steamrolling the market, but the monochrome display already looked archaic next to color competitors such as the Sega Game Gear or the Atari Lynx (which, however, paid the price in battery gluttony). The GBC chose a clever middle path: it added color, a somewhat faster processor and more memory, but kept low power consumption and, above all, **full backward compatibility** with the entire library of the original Game Boy. A new owner could thus play old and new games alike — and that was an argument the competition could not top. The lifespan of the GBC was nonetheless short, roughly three years before it was replaced by the Game Boy Advance in 2001. Even so, it managed to accumulate a remarkable library: the second generation of Pokémon (**Gold/Silver/Crystal**), a pair of excellent Zeldas (**Oracle of Seasons** and **Oracle of Ages**), Wario Land 3 and technically stunning titles from the end of the era. Among them stands out **Shantae**, which came out so late that it sold pitifully few copies — and today is extremely expensive for collectors. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the GBC is the 8-bit Sharp **LR35902** processor (a relative of the Z80 and the Intel 8080), which runs at double the frequency compared to the original Game Boy — roughly **8 MHz** in fast mode, whereas in compatible mode it runs slower like a classic GB. The working memory (RAM) and video RAM are both doubled compared to the predecessor (32 KB of system RAM, 16 KB of VRAM), which gave games more room for graphics. The display has a resolution of **160 × 144 pixels** and for the first time it is a color, reflective TFT panel. From a palette of **32,768 colors**, the GBC can display up to **56 colors** at once in a special mode — but typically **32 colors** (eight three-color palettes for backgrounds and eight for sprites, plus the transparency color). Sprites measure 8 × 8 or 8 × 16 pixels. The sound is provided by the same chip as in the original GB: **four channels** — two pulse channels (square wave), one wave channel with a programmable wave table and one noise channel for percussion and effects. The output is stereo to headphones. ### Connectivity and peripherals The GBC inherited the **Game Link** port for the connection cable — the basis of the famous Pokémon trades and battles as well as multiplayer in other titles. A novelty was the **infrared port (IR)** on the top edge of the console, which enabled wireless data exchange over a short distance; a handful of games used it, the best known being the trading of items in the Pokémon games and in the Zeldas. Cartridges carried backed-up memory (battery + SRAM) for saving progress, and some games even had a real-time clock — Pokémon Gold/Silver had a crystal **RTC** in the cartridge, whose battery unfortunately dries out over the years. Among the accessories, the **Game Boy Camera** and the **Game Boy Printer** are worth mentioning, both inherited from the GB era and fully functional with the GBC. Power was provided by two AA batteries with a life of around 10 hours, or an optionally purchasable mains adapter. ### Models and revisions The Game Boy Color came out in a single basic form, but in a wide palette of colored casing variants: the transparent "Atomic Purple", Berry, Grape, Kiwi, Dandelion, Teal and the classic Clear. In addition, there were limited editions — Japanese releases tied to specific titles as well as the iconic **Pokémon Edition** with a Pikachu motif. Games for the platform were divided into two categories according to the color of the cartridge. **Black cartridges** were "GBC-only" and worked exclusively on the Game Boy Color (and later the GBA). **Transparent/clear cartridges** were the so-called "dual mode" — color on the GBC, but also playable on the original black-and-white Game Boy, where they ran in shades of gray. The GBC hardware itself received no later internal display revision; its successor became only the entirely new Game Boy Advance architecture. ### Clones and variants The Game Boy as a brand was, thanks to its own encrypted boot and Nintendo-guarded licenses, harder to clone than, say, the NES, so fewer widespread hardware clones of the GBC were created than famiclones. Nevertheless, a number of **unofficial "pirate" cartridges** with unlicensed games and multi-game compilations appeared, widely seen also at markets in Eastern Europe and in Asia. While in Czechoslovakia the trace of Nintendo in the field of the handheld console is practically nonexistent (official distribution came only much later), the domestic clone scene manifested itself fully with other platforms — with 8-bit computers it was the **Didaktik** as a domestic clone of the ZX Spectrum, and with the console Nintendo, **famiclones** of the Pegasus type made their way into the region. The Game Boy Color reached Czech players mainly through imports and the gray market; however, the far cheaper imitation in the form of Chinese handheld consoles à la "Brick Game" became a legend of its time, though it had technically nothing in common with the GBC. ### Today's scene Emulation of the GBC is completely trouble-free today and is among the most rewarding of all. Top emulators such as **mGBA** or **SameBoy** achieve high accuracy including a faithful simulation of the LCD and the sound chip; on weaker devices **Gambatte** (a core in RetroArch) serves well. The GBC runs on practically anything — from phones through the Raspberry Pi all the way to pocket emulation consoles. The homebrew scene is also alive: developers today write new games in the C language via **GBDK** or in assembler and release them on real flash carts as well as ROMs to download. A symbol of this perseverance is the RPG **Infinity** — a commercial title whose development stalled around 2001 and which the original team completed after more than twenty years and released in 2023. A rare case of a "lost" game that came back to life.

game-boy-advance.history: When Nintendo unleashed the Game Boy Advance onto the world in 2001, it didn't just take another step in its handheld dynasty — it leapt across an entire generation. Where the Game Boy and Game Boy Color had built on an eight-bit heart from the late 1980s, the GBA delivered performance that in practice bordered on the level of the home Super Nintendo. Suddenly it was possible to carry games in your pocket that had once required a television and a big console sitting beneath it: ports of SNES classics, sprawling Japanese RPGs, full-fledged metroidvanias with dozens of hours of content. It sold over **80 million units**, and the GBA library remains to this day among the finest that handheld gaming has ever offered. An important trump card was also its **backward compatibility**: the GBA's wide slot accepted both Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, so the console functioned as one big pocket Nintendo arcade reaching all the way back to 1989. Alongside that it hosted its own gems — the trio of Castlevania titles (with **Aria of Sorrow** as the peak), Metroid Zero Mission and Fusion, Golden Sun, Advance Wars, the Mario & Luigi series, and Fire Emblem, which thanks to the GBA reached the West for the first time. ### Hardware: graphics and sound At the heart of the console was a 32-bit **ARM7TDMI** processor clocked at roughly 16.8 MHz, supplemented by an older Z80 core (Sharp LR35902) for backward compatibility with old games. The display had a resolution of **240 × 160 pixels** and could show up to 32,768 colors from a palette of over 32 thousand shades. Compared to the gray Game Boy, that was a chasm of difference. The graphics hardware offered several modes. In **tile-based** modes it handled up to four background layers with independent scrolling and typically **128 sprites**. Its true pride, however, was the so-called **Mode 7** style — affine transformations, meaning rotation and scaling of backgrounds and sprites directly in hardware. This gave rise to pseudo-3D effects, rotating maps, and zooms that were impossible at a purely software level. For 2D graphics it was an exceptionally capable machine. The sound was hybrid. The GBA inherited **four classic channels** from the original Game Boy (two pulse, one wave, and one noise), which it supplemented with two new **8-bit PCM (DMA) channels** for playing back digital samples. Music and digitized sounds could thus be mixed together, though the result typically had a slightly "compressed" character owing to the limited memory and sampling rate. Even so, a number of unforgettable soundtracks were created. ### Connectivity and peripherals The **Game Link cable** served for multiplayer gaming: up to four consoles could be connected, and in some titles a single cartridge sufficed for multiplayer mode (so-called single-pak). A link cable was also indispensable for trading and battling in Pokémon. Nintendo also offered a **Wireless Adapter**, bundled mainly with Pokémon FireRed/LeafGreen. An interesting bridge was the **GBA–GameCube link cable**, which connected the handheld to the home console — the GBA then served as a second screen or controller (famously with Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles or The Wind Waker). A hardware real-time clock (RTC) in some cartridges, for example in Pokémon Ruby/Sapphire, enabled an in-game day-and-night cycle. The original GBA had no backlit display, and a whole range of accessories like the **Worm Light** served to properly illuminate it. The joke that the most important peripheral is a little lamp had a real basis. ### Models and revisions The very first model (**AGB-001**, 2001) suffered from a notoriously known flaw: an **unlit display**. You could only play in good light. Nintendo fixed this with the **Game Boy Advance SP** model (**AGS-001**, 2003) with a folding design and front lighting (frontlight); the later **AGS-101** revision received a markedly better **backlit** display, today the most sought-after among collectors. The last piece in the family was the tiny **Game Boy Micro** (2005) with a beautiful backlit display, but at the cost of losing backward compatibility with old GB/GBC games and a smaller screen. For today's player on a retro console, incidentally, the absence of a backlight on the original is more of an advantage — modern displays show GBA games far better than the first model ever could. ### The scene today The GBA is today one of the most rewarding emulated platforms. The excellent open-source emulator **mGBA** runs accurately and undemandingly on practically everything — from PC through RetroArch to cheap Chinese handhelds with H700-series chips, where the games run absolutely smoothly. For enthusiasts there are also hardware FPGA solutions. The **homebrew and indie scene** is also alive: new titles like **Goodboy Galaxy** are being created, and even released on real cartridges for the original hardware. Thanks to the combination of JRPG depth, quality action, and games built for playing in bite-sized pieces, the Game Boy Advance remains for retro gamers a literal gold mine — and the prices of original games and consoles are now rising noticeably.

nds.history: When Nintendo unveiled a device with two screens at the end of 2004, one of them touch-sensitive, it sounded like a gamble. The competition, led by Sony and its glossy PSP, was betting on performance and multimedia; Nintendo instead came out with a "third pillar" that fit nowhere — and it became one of the **best-selling gaming systems of all time** with more than 150 million units. The **Nintendo DS** (short for both "Dual Screen" and "Developers' System") didn't bet on who had more pixels, but on how the games were played. And it won. The magic was in the interface. The lower **touch screen** was operated with a stylus or finger, plus a **microphone** and later even motion and other add-ons in cartridges. This opened the door to entirely new types of games and to players who until then had never picked up a controller — from brain training through caring for virtual puppies to drawing puzzle solutions directly on the screen. ### Hardware: two screens and a 3D chip Inside tick two ARM processors (ARM9 at ~67 MHz and ARM7 at ~33 MHz), which share the work. Each of the two **3" LCD screens** has a resolution of 256×192 dots; the lower one is resistive touch. The graphics combine 2D layers in the style of an advanced "GBA generation" with a separate **3D core** capable of textured polygons — this gave rise to titles like Super Mario 64 DS, Mario Kart DS, or Metroid Prime Hunters. The sound is handled by 16 channels and built-in stereo speakers. A big role is played by the **microphone** (blowing, voice inputs) and the **RTC clock**, on which games like Animal Crossing or the Pokémon day-and-night cycles were built. DS cartridges are small flash cards with their own save storage; slot 2 (GBA) additionally provided **backward compatibility** with the entire Game Boy Advance library and also served for accessories (Rumble Pak, Guitar Grip). ### Connectivity: touch, Wi-Fi, and local play The DS had built-in **Wi-Fi** from the start. Locally it was enough for just one player to own the game — via **Download Play** they sent out a demo version to nearby DS units and everyone played from one cartridge. The online service **Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection** was used by Mario Kart DS, Pokémon, or Tetris DS for matches over the internet (the official servers no longer run today, but the community has revived them through alternative servers). It is precisely **local multiplayer** that remains one of the reasons the DS stays popular to this day: all you need is a group with consoles within range and a single cartridge. ### Models and revisions The original "fat" model (2004) was soon replaced by the elegant **DS Lite** (2006) — thinner, lighter, and with markedly brighter displays; this is the model that sold the most. Next came the **DSi** (2008) with two cameras, its own DSiWare store, and a faster chip, but without a GBA slot. The **DSi XL** then offered large screens for more comfortable play. The line was finally replaced in 2011 by the **Nintendo 3DS** with backward compatibility and stereoscopic 3D. ### Clones and the gray zone The DS also became famous for **flash carts** (R4 and similar), which allowed running homebrew and backups — it was an enormous phenomenon that Nintendo fought unsuccessfully. For developers and enthusiasts, however, it also meant a rich **homebrew scene**: custom applications, emulators, and games written via devkitARM and the libnds library. ### The scene today DS emulation is mature today. On PC and mobile, **melonDS** reigns (accurate, with online support via alternative servers) alongside **DeSmuME**; on weaker hardware and handhelds the DS runs via cores in RetroArch. Playing with two screens is, on emulators, a matter of layout — side by side, one above the other, or one large and the other in a corner. On devices like Anbernic or Retroid the DS will run, but touch is replaced by a stylus on a touch display or by mapping to the right stick, so purely "stylus-based" games (Trauma Center, drawing) call for a few compromises. Even so, the DS library — from JRPGs through Castlevania to Ace Attorney — is one of the richest and most timeless that retro gaming offers. ### What to play the DS on today: emulators and handhelds The DS belongs to the **undemanding systems**, so almost anything will run it — the catch isn't in performance, but in how to solve the **two screens and touch**. Here is a practical overview: - **PC (the best experience):** reach for **melonDS** — it's accurate, snappy, and even has restored **online multiplayer** via alternative servers (Wi-Mmproxy/Kaeru). An older but still functional choice is **DeSmuME**. Both also run within **RetroArch** (the melonDS core). You handle touch with the mouse, and lay out the two screens side by side, one above the other, or one large and the other in a corner. - **Android phone / tablet:** an ideal combination, because the **touch screen stands in for the stylus**. **melonDS** reigns (free) alongside the commercial **DraStic** (very fast). On powerful Android the DS runs without trouble even with upscaling. - **Android retro handhelds (Retroid Pocket, Odin, AYN):** excellent — they have a touch display, so stylus games work naturally, and there's plenty of power even for 3D titles like Mario Kart DS or Metroid Prime Hunters. - **Anbernic / Linux handhelds (RG35XX and the like):** the DS will run via RetroArch, but it's a **compromise** — weaker units with the Allwinner H700 handle 2D games decently, while 3D already stutters. Above all, though, comfortable touch is missing: you control the lower screen either on the (often non-touch) display, or mapped to the right stick. - **R36S and the cheapest boxes:** the DS is **on the edge** here — the RK3326 only manages simpler 2D games and touch is annoying. For the DS, better choose an Android device or PC. **Whether it works:** yes, and easily — just pick your device according to the games. For **JRPGs, visual novels, and 2D platformers** (Pokémon, Castlevania, Ace Attorney) anything will do; for **3D and stylus games** reach for Android or PC, where both touch and performance fit best. **Why know it:** the Nintendo DS showed that innovation in control can beat raw performance — and it left behind a library full of games you won't find anywhere else.

3ds.history:
After the triumph of the DS, Nintendo decided that the next step would be into the third dimension — and quite literally so. The **Nintendo 3DS** (2011) brought **glasses-free stereoscopic 3D**: thanks to a parallax barrier, the top screen could render depth just like that, simply by looking at it. It was a bold, slightly crazy idea that ultimately became more of an interesting bonus than the main draw — because the real treasure of the 3DS turned out to be, just like with the DS, its **library**. Despite a rocky start (a high price that Nintendo soon slashed dramatically), the console sold tens of millions of units and hosts some of the best games of its generation.

The 3DS built on the DS with its pair of screens and touch input, but added a hefty performance leap, a **3D camera**, motion sensors and an online ecosystem. And crucially it was **backward compatible with the DS** — the entire huge DS library can be played on it too.

### Technology: glasses-free 3D and decent performance

At its heart is a dual-core **ARM11** paired with a **PICA200** graphics chip, which handles full 3D with lighting and effects — that's why games like Super Mario 3D Land, Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D or Monster Hunter look surprisingly rich on the small screen. The top display (400×240 per eye, twice that for the 3D effect) shows a stereoscopic image, while the lower 320×240 one is a touchscreen. The strength of the 3D effect is adjusted with the **3D Slider** — it can even be turned off completely, which most players ended up doing over time anyway.

### Connectivity: StreetPass, SpotPass and online

The 3DS had clever social features. **StreetPass** exchanged data with the consoles of passers-by (Mii, moves in Puzzle Swap, ghosts in games), while **SpotPass** downloaded content over Wi-Fi in the background. Online play through the **Nintendo Network** served for multiplayer as well as the **eShop** store (which was closed in 2023, though games already purchased remain playable). Local wireless play and Download Play worked much like on the DS.

### Models and revisions

The family is varied: the original **3DS** was followed by the large **3DS XL**, then the cheap **2DS** (a flat wedge without the 3D effect, ideal for children), the elegant **New 3DS / New 3DS XL** (2014) with a second stick (the C-stick), a more powerful chip and colourful interchangeable covers, and finally the **New 2DS XL**. Some later games (e.g. Xenoblade Chronicles 3D) ran **only on the "New" models**.

### Clones and homebrew

Official clones don't exist, but the **homebrew scene** is exceptionally lively: via entry points like *ninjhax* and later the *Luma3DS* custom firmware, the community opened the door to its own applications, emulators, translations and improvements. The 3DS thus also became a popular "pocket emulation" console for older systems.

### Where to play the 3DS today: emulators and consoles

The 3DS is **more demanding to emulate** than the DS, but today it's a solved problem. On PC, **Citra** reigns (or rather its successors and forks after the project was discontinued — Lime3DS, Azahar), which handles most games even with upscaling to high resolution and smoothing — paradoxically making the games look better than on the original. It also works **on powerful Android** (Citra MMJ and its successors), so Android handhelds like the **Retroid Pocket** or **Odin** run it decently. Weaker Linux handhelds (Anbernic H700, R36S) **basically can't handle** the 3DS — this is the domain of more powerful hardware. The most authentic experience is of course offered by the **original console with custom firmware**, where you can additionally run the entire DS library.

**Why you should know it:** The Nintendo 3DS combined a crazy idea (glasses-free 3D) with one of the strongest game libraries of its generation — from Zelda through Pokémon to Monster Hunter — and on top of that it can run the whole DS catalogue too.

nes.history: When the North American gaming market lay in ruins in the mid-1980s, few would have bet that video games would once again take over children's bedrooms all around the world. The crash of 1983, stores flooded with low-quality titles and the symbolic burial of unsold ET cartridges in the Texas desert sent a clear signal: entertainment on the television screen was a finished fad. And then came Nintendo. Its **Famicom** (Family Computer), which appeared in Japan in 1983, and its Western redesign the **NES** (Nintendo Entertainment System, USA 1985, Europe 1986/87) quite literally resurrected the entire industry. The key wasn't just the technology, but above all **quality control**. Nintendo introduced a strict licensing system with its famous "Nintendo Seal of Quality" and limited the number of titles a publisher could release per year — a direct reaction to what had killed the market before. The bundled **Super Mario Bros.** then showed what a perfect platformer should look like and became synonymous with games in general. The console ultimately sold over 60 million units and raised an entire generation of players and creators alike. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the NES is the eight-bit **Ricoh 2A03** processor (2A07 in the PAL version), built on a core compatible with the MOS 6502, into which Nintendo also integrated the sound unit. It runs at roughly 1.79 MHz (NTSC). The image is handled by a separate graphics chip, the **PPU (Picture Processing Unit)**, which manages a resolution of 256×240 pixels. From a total palette of 54 usable colours (64 values are often cited, some of which repeat), up to 25 colours can be put on screen at once, divided into palettes of four. The PPU handles hardware **sprites** — a maximum of 64 sprites in total and 8 per line, which is why in older games the sprites flicker when overloaded. Smooth hardware **scrolling** of the background was a given, something Super Mario Bros. made famous. The sound chip offers five channels: two pulse (square) channels, one triangle channel for bass, a noise channel for percussion and a simple channel for sampled sound (DPCM). The characteristic "blip" melodies of composers like Koji Kondo were forever etched into collective memory. Many cartridges also contained additional **mappers** — chips that expanded memory addressing as well as graphics and sound capabilities. That's why late games like **Kirby's Adventure** or **Mega Man 3** look and sound significantly better than the early titles. ### Connectivity and peripherals The NES had a rich array of accessories. The console came with the **Zapper** light gun controller (the legendary Duck Hunt) and the **R.O.B.** robot, which played more of a marketing role at launch. For more players there was the **NES Four Score** adapter (and in Japan, controller sockets right on the Famicom). The Famicom also differed from the NES in its connectors: it had hardwired controllers, the second of which carried a microphone, and an expansion port for peripherals such as the **Famicom Disk System** floppy drive. In Japan the **Famicom Modem** also worked for online services. The North American NES sent its image via an RF modulator or a composite AV output; the later AV Famicom model added a higher-quality composite signal. ### Models and revisions The original American NES (model **NES-001**) had its iconic "toaster" design with a front slide-in slot and a **ZIF** press-down mechanism. It was precisely this mechanism that, over the years, became the cause of the notorious image flickering, as the contacts oxidised. In 1993 a compact redesign, the **NES-101** (the so-called "top loader"), came out with a top slot that eliminated the contact problems, though it lacked a composite output. In Japan Nintendo released the elegant **AV Famicom (HVC-101)** in 1993. Much later the miniature **NES Classic Edition** (2016) with emulated games also appeared. ### Clones and variants The NES is among the most cloned consoles of all time. Around the world, especially in the Eastern Bloc and Asia, unlicensed **famiclones** circulated. In Central and Eastern Europe the best known was the **Pegasus** — a famiclone sold from the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, which even in Czechoslovakia became the very first console for many children, because the original Nintendo was unavailable and expensive. These clones used hardware compatible with the Famicom and often came with multi-game cartridges. ### Today's scene NES emulation is completely solved today — accurate emulators like **Mesen** or the **Nestopia** and **FCEUX** cores (often within RetroArch) run even on the weakest hardware. At the same time, the NES homebrew scene is probably the liveliest of all retro platforms. The tools and community have matured to such a degree that games like **Micro Mages** or **Lizard** are being made that look and play better than most period titles — and are even released on actual cartridges. For many creators the NES remains a dream platform precisely because of those "beautiful limitations" that force clever and honest design.

snes.history: When Nintendo unveiled the Super Famicom in Japan in 1990 (marketed in the West from 1991 as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System), it was not a race to be first. Sega had already been selling its sixteen-bit Mega Drive for a year and was needling the competition with the word “Nintendon't.” Nintendo nonetheless took its time and bet on something other than speed: on color, on sound, and on graphical tricks that turned the screen into a little theater. Many today consider the result to be the **pinnacle of 2D game design** overall and one of the most beloved machines in history. The “console wars” duel between Sega and Nintendo was the first great marketing war of the gaming industry and defined the entire 1990s. Sega sold speed and a more grown-up image built around Sonic, while Nintendo sold depth and the quality of its library. It is that very library that makes the SNES a legend: the best platformers of their day (Super Mario World, Donkey Kong Country, Yoshi's Island), genre-defining JRPGs (Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy VI, Secret of Mana), and the metroidvania bible Super Metroid. These are titles that still appear on lists of the best games of all time. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the console is the sixteen-bit Ricoh 5A22 processor, built on a core compatible with the 65C816 and clocked variably up to roughly 3.58 MHz. Graphics are handled by a pair of PPU chips, which can manage a palette of **32,768 colors** and conjure hundreds of them onto the screen at once. The console offered several graphics modes with varying numbers of background layers and color depths, hardware interlaced scrolling, and sprite management. The most famous trump card is **Mode 7** — a mode that can rotate, enlarge, and shrink a single background layer in real time. This is the source of the pseudo-3D curving track in Super Mario Kart and F-Zero, or the map unfurling in the finale of Final Fantasy VI. On top of that, the SNES could do effects such as semi-transparency and color blending, which made the image feel softer and richer than the competition's. Sound is a chapter of its own. It is handled by a **sound subsystem designed by Sony** (Ken Kutaragi, later the father of the PlayStation) — the SPC700 control chip together with the DSP manages **eight channels** playing sampled sound with ADPCM processing and hardware echo or reverb. That is why the soundtracks of games like Chrono Trigger or Donkey Kong Country still sound exceptionally full and melodic to this day. ### Connectivity and peripherals The standard SNES gamepad added to the proven D-pad a set of four action buttons, two shoulder buttons L and R, and of course Start and Select — a scheme that influenced all later controllers. The console had two ports; for more players there was the **Multitap** splitter (for example NHL or Bomberman). Among the peripherals worth mentioning are the **Super Scope** light gun, a wireless, bazooka-like colossus powered by batteries, and — unusually for Nintendo — the **SNES Mouse**, supplied with the drawing program Mario Paint. A famous chapter is the never-released CD add-on developed with Sony; after a falling-out, it eventually gave rise to the standalone PlayStation. For video, the console output through a multi-pin connector supporting composite as well as better S-Video and RGB signals. A specialty of the platform are the **add-on chips right inside the cartridges**, which upgraded the machine. The most famous is the **Super FX** (3D polygons in Star Fox and Stunt Race FX), and also the SA-1, DSP-1 (Pilotwings, Super Mario Kart), or the SuperFX2 in Yoshi's Island. Some games at the end of the console's life looked as if they belonged on an entirely different platform. ### Models and revisions The console's design differed by region: the Japanese Super Famicom and the European/Australian SNES had rounded shapes and colored buttons, while the North American version got a more angular gray coat with purple buttons. Later came a shrunken and cheaper redesign — in the USA as the **SNES (model SNS-101, the “Jr.”)**, in Japan as the Super Famicom Jr. These later versions, however, no longer had RGB output or the threaded holes for the feet. The hardware also existed in semi-official versions for developers and arcades (the Super System for arcades). It is worth knowing for collectors that, because of copy protection, even the shapes of the cartridge slots differed between regions. ### Clones and variants The SNES did not experience as sprawling a clone scene as the NES with its famiclones, yet unofficial compatible machines did appear, especially in Asia and later also cheap “retro” consoles. In the Czech and Czechoslovak environment, the SNES was, compared to eight-bit computers, more of a rare imported curiosity — while the ZX Spectrum had the domestic Didaktik clone and the NES circulated as the Pegasus, the sixteen-bit Nintendo mostly arrived here through unofficial imports and was expensive. Only in later years did it become more accessible, and today it is a prized piece among domestic collectors. ### The scene today SNES emulation is very well mastered today — the reference is the accurate **bsnes/higan**, while for ordinary play **Snes9x** is more than enough, both also available as cores for RetroArch. On more powerful handheld devices (for example those with the H700 chip) it runs reliably; only the most demanding titles with add-on chips can occasionally cause trouble. Nintendo itself offers a selection of games as part of Switch Online and earlier via the mini-console Super NES Classic Edition. The **homebrew and fan scene** is alive as well: modern titles such as **The Curse of Issyos** are being created, fans polish translations of Japanese exclusives, and romhacks add new content to the classics. Thanks to this, the Super Nintendo remains a thoroughly living platform even after more than thirty years.

mega-drive.history: At the end of the 1980s, Nintendo dominated the gaming world so decisively that it seemed unbeatable. But then Sega arrived with a console that had an entirely different temperament. The **Mega Drive** (sold in North America as the **Genesis**) arrived in Japan in 1988, in America a year later, and in Europe in 1990. Sega bet on speed, cheek, and the image of a “cool” alternative for an older audience — and for a while it had the 16-bit market practically to itself, because the Super Nintendo arrived only later. The symbol of this philosophy became **Sonic the Hedgehog**. Where Mario was measured and good-natured, Sonic was about speed, attitude, and self-confidence. The famous American slogan “Genesis does what Nintendon't” summed up the whole strategy: to be faster, more grown-up, and more willing to go to the edge. Symbolic was the affair around the game **Mortal Kombat** — while the SNES version censored the blood, on the Genesis it could be unlocked by entering a code, which earned Sega no small number of points with teenagers. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the console is the **Motorola 68000** processor clocked at roughly 7.6 MHz — the same CPU family that powers the Amiga and early Macintoshes. Sound and compatibility were also handled by an auxiliary eight-bit **Zilog Z80**, which could drive the sound subsystem (and in compatibility mode also run games for the older Master System). The graphics run at a resolution of around **320×224** pixels. From a palette of **512 colors**, 61 colors can be displayed at once (four palettes of sixteen, with zero as transparent) — that was a noticeable disadvantage compared to the later SNES and the reason why games on the Mega Drive tend to have a bolder, higher-contrast palette. In motion, on the other hand, the console excelled: the hardware handled two scrolling layers plus a sprite layer and allowed **up to 80 sprites** on screen, which is why brisk games like Sonic, Streets of Rage, or Gunstar Heroes keep their pace even in the greatest chaos. Sound is handled by the **Yamaha YM2612** FM chip with six FM channels, supplemented by the **SN76489** chip with three tones and noise. The result is the characteristic “harsher,” synthetic sound that gave rise to legendary soundtracks — for example Yuzo Koshiro's music for **Streets of Rage 2**. ### Connectivity and peripherals The Mega Drive caters to multiplayer — it has **two controller ports**, and the original gamepad had three buttons; later the popular **six-button** model was added because of fighting games like Street Fighter II. For fans of racing and sports there was the **Team Player** splitter (i.e. the 4-Player Adaptor) allowing play for up to four players. Among the accessories worth mentioning are the **Menacer** light gun, the **SEGA Activator** peripheral that captured motion, and, on the Japanese version, a modem for the Sega Meganet service. The console connected to the television via RF or composite/RGB output; on the first models there was also a headphone output with volume control on the front panel. ### Models and revisions Sega released several hardware versions. The original **Model 1** (1988) had that headphone jack and, on the oldest units, the inscription “High Definition Graphics.” The slimmer and cheaper **Model 2** (1993) dropped the headphone output and simplified the sound circuitry (it became known for a slightly different, “drier” sound). There was also the compact **Model 3** from Majesco and, later, licensed redesigns. The system also had add-ons: the **Sega CD** (in Japan the Mega-CD) added a CD drive and games with full-fledged sound and video sequences, while the **32X** was a 32-bit power add-on mounted onto the cartridge slot. Both add-ons rather flopped commercially and are today a reminder of how Sega gradually lost its lead position. ### Clones and variants The Mega Drive is one of the few older consoles whose clones are still being manufactured today. After the patents expired, cheap variants flooded the market — the best known are the **AtGames** models (the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive Classic line with preinstalled games), Chinese handhelds, and all-in-one consoles. In Brazil the license is held by the company **Tectoy**, which has been selling the Mega Drive continuously for decades, released local exclusives, and even took it as far as its own new revisions — Brazil is thus the largest living bastion of this console. In Czechoslovakia and the wider Eastern Bloc, the Mega Drive was, because of its price and import barriers, not as widespread as eight-bit computers; it came to the fore rather only in the 1990s through gray imports and later precisely through cheap clones. ### The scene today Mega Drive emulation is completely mature today — cores like **Genesis Plus GX** run reliably even on weak hardware, and on modern retro handhelds the games run smoothly. Remarkable, however, is above all the **homebrew scene**, which is among the most impressive of all. Technically advanced new releases such as **Demons of Asteborg**, **Xeno Crisis**, or the atmospheric **Tanglewood** keep appearing, sometimes even on real cartridges. Because Sega rather tolerates the community, the scene flourishes, and so the Mega Drive is still alive thirty-five years after its launch.

master-system.history: The SEGA Master System is something of a forgotten hero of the eight-bit era. When SEGA launched it in Japan in 1985 (as the Sega Mark III, later renamed) and a year later in the United States, it pitted the machine directly against Nintendo and its NES. It lost the battle for the North American and Japanese markets decisively — Nintendo had locked up most third-party developers with tough licensing contracts, so the Master System was a technically decent console left with empty software shelves. But then there is Europe and Brazil. Here the story flips. On the old continent, where Nintendo was far from having such a head start, the Master System made a strong mark and became the first console for an entire generation of players. And in Brazil, where distribution was taken over by the company Tectoy, the platform lived on for an incredibly long time — new games, variants and redesigns kept appearing there well into the new millennium. For retro gamers, the Master System is a likeable discovery: it feels like "a better NES that nobody remembered". ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the console is the eight-bit **Zilog Z80** processor running at roughly 3.58 MHz — the same family known to owners of the ZX Spectrum or MSX. Graphics are handled by the **VDP** video chip derived from the Texas Instruments TMS9918, which SEGA significantly improved. The result is a resolution of **256×192 pixels** and a palette of **64 colors**, of which up to **32 can be shown on screen at once** (two palettes of sixteen). Compared to the NES, which made do with noticeably poorer and often "dirty" coloring, this was a tangible step forward — Master System games look richer and cleaner. The hardware could handle **up to 64 sprites** with smooth background scrolling, which the ports of SEGA arcade titles put to good use. The weak point, on the other hand, was sound: the basic **SN76489** (PSG) chip offers three tone channels and one noise channel. It is functional, but compared to the competition it is more of a beep. The Japanese version and Japanese cartridges additionally supported an expansion with the **Yamaha YM2413** chip (FM synthesis), so a title run on a Japanese Master System sounded a class richer than the same game on a European console. ### Connectivity and peripherals The Master System had a varied range of accessories for its time. The best known is the **Light Phaser** — a light gun for shooters such as Safari Hunt or Rambo III. The pinnacle, however, was the **SegaScope 3-D Glasses**, active shutter glasses for stereoscopic 3D in a handful of titles (Zaxxon 3-D, Maze Hunter 3-D). In the mid-eighties this was a remarkably bold experiment. An interesting solution was the dual media format: alongside classic cartridges, the console also read thin **Sega Cards** (My Card) for cheaper, smaller games. Standard features were two controller ports, a separate Pause button right on the console, and on the first model a built-in game in memory. The picture was connected via RF or composite AV. ### Models and revisions The original **Master System** (1986) was a bulky black box with control buttons and a card slot. In 1990 came the **Master System II** — a cheaper and smaller redesign that dropped the card slot, the reset button and the connector for the 3D glasses, and instead of Snail Maze it usually had an eight-bit **Alex Kidd in Miracle World** built in (Sonic in some regions). The Japanese base was formed by the **Sega Mark III** with the option of an FM sound unit. In Brazil, an endless range of its own variants emerged under the Tectoy brand — from portable versions to models with hundreds of pre-installed games, released long after the platform had long been dead elsewhere in the world. ### Clones and variants The Master System shares the vast majority of its hardware and library with the handheld **Game Gear** — which is essentially a portable Master System with a backlit display, so both platforms are emulated practically together today. Brazil's Tectoy additionally produced licensed clones and continued local development. For Czech and Czechoslovak players it is fair to admit that the Master System was not as widespread here as the ZX Spectrum that dominated our market and its clone the **Didaktik**, nor as the later NES-based famiclones such as the Pegasus. Even so, in Europe generally it made a much more visible mark than in the USA, so nostalgic memories of it are stronger here than across the ocean. ### Today's scene Emulating the Master System is trivial today — practically any device can handle it, including cheap Chinese handhelds. The library has its gems: the pioneering RPG **Phantasy Star** with 3D dungeons, the excellent **Wonder Boy** series (especially The Dragon's Trap), the eight-bit Sonic line, and SEGA's original mascot **Alex Kidd**. Many other titles were arcade ports such as Shinobi, Space Harrier or Fantasy Zone. The platform is moreover still alive on the creative side: modern homebrew is being released, for example the platformer **Devwill Too**, and not infrequently even physically on new cartridges. The Master System thus remains an ideal choice for anyone who has the NES classics behind them and wants to get to know the eight-bit era from a different, more richly colored angle.

game-gear.history: When Sega introduced the Game Gear in 1990 (a year later in Europe and the USA), it entered a battle that Nintendo had long since started with its Game Boy. Sega, however, was betting on one trump card that its rival lacked: a **color backlit display**. While the Game Boy offered only four shades of greenish gray, the Game Gear glowed in full color and looked like a pocket television. Sega's marketing pushed this difference to the extreme, and for a moment it seemed handheld gaming would take on a whole new dimension. Under the hood there was nothing new. The Game Gear was essentially a **Master System crammed into a pocket case** — it shared the same processor, the same graphics and sound chip, and to a large extent its game library too. This kinship was both its strength (fast porting of titles) and the reason it never caught up with the technological bar later set by 16-bit machines. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the console is the eight-bit **Zilog Z80** processor clocked at around 3.5 MHz — the same proven core that powered the Master System and the ZX Spectrum. Graphics are provided by a derivative of the **VDP** chip from the Master System. The display has a resolution of **160 × 144 pixels**, the same area as the Game Boy, but with a completely different look: out of a palette of **4096 colors** the Game Gear can show **up to 32 colors at once** (typically split into two palettes of sixteen). Against its monochrome rival this is a chasm of a difference. The hardware handles hardware **sprites** and smooth **scrolling** across the entire area, so action games, platformers and shmups run briskly. Because the screen is smaller than the Master System's TV output, many ports were slightly **cropped** — the field of view narrowed so that objects would stay large and legible enough. Sound is handled by the classic **SN76489** (PSG) with **three tone channels and one noise channel**. Through the built-in speaker it sounds rather tinny, but through headphones the Game Gear additionally offered a **stereo output** — a pleasant bonus the Master System did not have by default. ### Connectivity and peripherals The Game Gear also thought about two-player games. Using the **Gear-to-Gear link cable** you could connect two consoles and play multiplayer, for example races in *Sonic Drift 2*. Each player, however, needed their own unit and their own copy of the game. The most famous accessory, though, was the **TV Tuner** — an add-on that turned the console into a **pocket color television**. It was a period curiosity hit and today a sought-after collector's item. There was also the **Master Gear Converter (Master System Converter)**, which let you run Master System cartridges on the Game Gear, as well as an **AV/TV output** solution and a mains adapter that partially addressed the dreaded battery consumption. And it was the batteries that were the Achilles' heel. The Game Gear devoured **six AA batteries** in just three to four hours, while the Game Boy ran on four cells for over ten hours. The nickname **"battery guzzler"** has stuck with it to this day. ### Models and revisions Sega also released a **smaller and lighter redesign** of the console, which reduced the dimensions compared to the original bulky body. There were also colored case variants for different markets. Years later, the Game Gear even got an official "comeback" in miniature form: in 2020 Sega released the **Game Gear Micro** for the company's anniversary — a tiny replica with a minuscule screen and a few pre-installed games, aimed more at collectors and fans than at actual playing. A serious sore point of every original unit today is **cracked capacitors** in both the sound and picture sections. Many surviving consoles therefore need a so-called **recap** — a complete replacement of the capacitors — to bring back sound and a clean picture. ### Clones and variants Around the Game Gear there never grew such a jungle of clones as around the NES or the ZX Spectrum, where famiclones (Pegasus) or the Czechoslovak **Didaktik** appeared in the East. Sega held the hardware more firmly in its own hands. The key "variants" are therefore mainly official ones: the aforementioned redesign, the **Game Gear Micro**, and further the link to the home world via the **Master Gear Converter**, thanks to which the handheld effectively became a portable Master System. Collector's interest then lies in regional versions and packaging (Sega vs. licensed distributors in individual countries). ### Today's scene For today's retro gamer the Game Gear is ideal precisely because its one big weakness — battery consumption — disappears on an emulator. Emulators such as **Emulicious**, **MEKA**, **BlastEm** or universal cores in **RetroArch** run the library without problems and, on top of that, with a smooth color picture. The library ranges from eight-bit **Sonics** (*Sonic Triple Trouble*, *Sonic Chaos*) through the exploratory spin-off **Tails Adventure**, close to a metroidvania, to the excellent shmups of the **GG Aleste** line. The best proof that the platform is alive is the game **GG Aleste 3** by the renowned studio **M2** from 2020 — a brand-new title for a long-"dead" handheld, released as part of the *Aleste Collection*. The Game Gear thus turned from a loser of its time into a pleasant island to explore.

atari-lynx.history: When Atari unveiled the Lynx in 1989, it looked like a sure-fire hit: the world's first handheld console with a **color backlit LCD display**. While Nintendo came out the same year with the Game Boy and its greenish shades of gray, the Lynx showed full color, could scale and rotate sprites in hardware and thus created pseudo-3D effects the Game Boy could not even dream of. Technically it was a machine a whole class more advanced. Yet the design did not originate at Atari itself — the console was originally developed by Epyx under the name **Handy**, and Atari subsequently bought it and brought it to market. People who had previously been behind Atari's famous arcade machines worked on its development, and that shows across the whole library. The Lynx's story is, however, a textbook example of the fact that better technology alone is not enough. The console ultimately lost, and the Game Boy swept it away in sales. There were essentially three reasons: the high price (almost twice that of the Game Boy), the impractical size and weight, and above all its **battery appetite**. The Lynx drained six AA batteries in some three to four hours of play, whereas the Game Boy comfortably ran on four batteries for over ten hours. For a portable device that was a fatal weakness. Nintendo also held a trump card in the form of Tetris and incomparably stronger software support. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the Lynx was an 8-bit processor derived from the proven **MOS 65C02** running at roughly 4 MHz, supported by Atari's own chips (known as Mikey and Suzy). It was the Suzy graphics coprocessor that handled the most interesting part: it could **scale, distort and rotate sprites** in hardware, which enabled smooth zooming in and out of objects and a simple illusion of space. This capability made games like Blue Lightning or S.T.U.N. Runner a spectacular sight that competing handhelds could not manage. The display showed a resolution of **160 × 102 pixels** and could render up to 16 colors simultaneously from a palette of 4096 shades. The backlight was a luxury in 1989 — you could play in the dark too, which was simply impossible on the Game Boy. Sound was handled by the Mikey chip with **four channels** and support for stereo output, so through headphones the Lynx played noticeably richer than the beeping competition. ### Connectivity and peripherals The flagship feature was the **ComLynx** network link: with a special cable you could connect up to **eight consoles** into a single multiplayer session, which was a rarity for its time. Part of the library took full advantage of it — the races of RoadBlasters or California Games were an experience with more people. The hardware itself was clever too. The console could be **rotated in software**, so the picture flipped and left-handed players could comfortably operate the machine — the button layout adapted. Games were distributed on small cartridges, and Atari also offered accessories such as a network adapter or a sun shade for the display that helped with readability in direct light. ### Models and revisions The Lynx saw two main hardware versions. The original **Lynx I** from 1989 was large, angular and swallowed batteries mercilessly. In 1991 came the redesigned **Lynx II**: it was smaller and lighter, gained a headphone output with stereo sound, a switchable backlight to save energy and a practical sliding display cover. Games were fully compatible between both models, so it was purely a redesign aimed at better ergonomics and longer endurance. ### Clones and variants Thanks to its custom chips, the Lynx has no classic unofficial clones of the kind we know from, say, the NES or the ZX Spectrum — the hardware could not be easily imitated. Its legacy thus lives on not in imitations, but in its **library of arcade ports**. Many titles were faithful conversions of Atari and Midway arcade machines: Robotron, RoadBlasters, S.T.U.N. Runner, Xybots or Rygar. Roughly 40% of the games were released exclusively for the Lynx, which today makes them prized collector's items and a reason why the console retains a cult status among fans. ### Today's scene For retro gamers the Lynx is great news. In emulation its only fundamental flaw — the battery gobbling — disappears entirely, and only the beautiful color display and solid arcade library remain. The most widespread solution is the **Handy** core within libretro/RetroArch, which runs reliably even on weaker pocket devices and modern handhelds. The Lynx thus finally gets the appreciation it never earned in its own time. It is remarkable that the scene around the Lynx is still alive. The regular **Atari Gamer** competition brings new homebrew titles, and ambitious modern projects are also emerging, such as the JRPG **Wyvern Tales**. The Atari Lynx is ultimately one of the finest proofs that a commercial defeat does not yet mean the end — it just happened a few decades earlier than the world was able to appreciate it.

saturn.history: The SEGA Saturn is a tragic hero of gaming history. When Sega launched it in Japan in November 1994, it was an ambitious machine built on a series of processors — a symbol that Sega wanted to enter the 3D era at full force. But it was precisely this force that turned out to be a curse. In the American market the console was buried by the legendary moment at the E3 trade show in May 1995, where Sega announced a surprise immediate sale for 399 dollars — a move that angered retailers and developers alike and from which the Saturn never recovered in the West. In Japan, however, it was quite a different story: there the console did decently, received dozens of exclusives and to this day is a sought-after treasure among collectors and connoisseurs. It hides gems such as **Panzer Dragoon Saga**, **Radiant Silvergun** or **Dragon Force**. ### Technology: graphics and sound The Saturn's architecture is notorious for its complexity. At its heart are **two 32-bit Hitachi SH-2 processors** clocked at 28.6 MHz, complemented by two graphics chips, **VDP1** (responsible for sprites, polygons and rendering) and **VDP2** (background layers and scrolling). Add to that a control processor and a sound subsystem — so in total the machine contains an impressive count of eight processors. This multi-chip philosophy made the Saturn a master of **2D graphics**: it handled a huge number of sprites, practically unlimited background layers and smooth scrolling, thanks to which it delivered the best home ports of the arcade 2D games of its time. The catch lay in 3D. The VDP1 did not work with triangles but with **quadrilateral sprites (quads)**, which was a completely different approach than the one the competition chose. Programming 3D scenes was therefore unintuitive and demanding, and moreover few people knew how to split the load between two CPUs without a shared cache. When Sony released the technically more elegant and easily programmable PlayStation, many developers rather bypassed the Saturn. Sound was handled by the **Yamaha SCSP (Saturn Custom Sound Processor)** driven by its own Motorola 68EC000. It offered **32 PCM/FM channels** and quality digital sound that matched the competition and positively shone in musically strong titles (such as **NiGHTS into Dreams...**). ### Connectivity and peripherals The Saturn had a rich accessory ecosystem. On the front it carried **two controller ports**, to which the iconic **3D Control Pad** with an analog stick and analog triggers connected — it was created precisely for the game NiGHTS and foreshadowed modern controls. Sega also offered a steering wheel, arcade sticks and, for shooters, the **Virtua Gun (Stunner)** light gun. A very important element were the **expansion cartridges** slotted into the port on the top side. Besides a memory card for saving positions, these were mainly **RAM cartridges (1 MB and 4 MB)**, which dramatically improved the ports of demanding 2D fighting games by Capcom and SNK — without them **X-Men vs. Street Fighter**, for instance, would never have run so faithfully on the Saturn. For network gaming there was the **SegaNet** modem in Japan and NetLink in the West. Video output covered composite, S-Video and RGB SCART, so the Saturn ranks among the best-looking consoles of its generation on a quality display. ### Models and revisions The console went through several redesigns. The original **Japanese model was gray**, whereas it arrived in the West in a **sober black** variant. The hardware gradually got cheaper: early boards had a pair of separate chips, later revisions integrated them. The most visible change was the transition from round buttons and an oval connector on the first units to **oval/rounded buttons** and a cheaper design in later series. A curiosity is the **HiSaturn** and **V-Saturn** — licensed variants made by Hitachi and JVC (Victor), which technically matched the Sega and differed only in the brand and the box. Hitachi even went so far as to produce a portable hybrid version with an LCD and car navigation (HiSaturn Navi). ### Clones and variants Genuine unofficial clones of the Saturn practically do not exist — the architecture was too complex and expensive for anyone to imitate, unlike the simple NES. In former **Czechoslovakia** the Saturn was not officially sold and reached the market only through imports, so neither the gray nor the black Saturn was a common part of children's rooms like, say, the Pegasus famiclones among the 8-bit machines. As "variants" we therefore count rather the above-mentioned licensed versions **V-Saturn (JVC)** and **HiSaturn (Hitachi)** and the regional editions (Japan, North America, Europe) with different regional locks, because of which switches and modding chips are still used to this day. ### Today's scene Emulation of the Saturn is among the most demanding of all — precisely because of the eight-processor architecture. For years it was inaccurate, but today it is decently handled by emulators such as **Mednafen/Beetle Saturn**, **Yabause** and its modern successor **Kronos** or **SSF**. On weaker hardware (for example the H700 chips in portable Anbernics) mainly 2D titles run reliably, while demanding 3D games need more powerful devices. The community has also revived thanks to **ODE drives** (optical drive emulator, e.g. Fenrir or Satiator), which replace the aging CD drive with an SD card. Homebrew and translations of Japanese exclusives into English also flourish, so the treasures the Saturn offers are more accessible today than ever before.

playstation.history: When Sony launched its first gaming machine in Japan in December 1994, few suspected that this was the beginning of the end of an era in which the gaming market was split between Nintendo and Sega. The **PlayStation** paradoxically emerged from the wreckage of a failed partnership — Sony was originally preparing a CD add-on for the Super Nintendo, but Nintendo cancelled the collaboration at the last minute and struck a deal with Philips. Humiliated but determined, Sony transformed its project into a standalone console and used it to defeat both reigning kings. The key to its success was betting on **CD-ROM** instead of expensive cartridges. This meant cheaper manufacturing, many times greater capacity (cinematic cutscenes, voice acting, quality music) and a lower barrier for studios. On top of that, Sony treated developers well and built a „more grown-up“ image of gaming aimed at teenagers and young adults. The result? More than 100 million units sold and a generation that defined modern gaming. **Final Fantasy VII** popularised JRPGs in the West, **Resident Evil** and **Silent Hill** created the survival horror genre, **Metal Gear Solid** and **Tomb Raider** showcased the power of 3D storytelling, and **Gran Turismo** elevated racing simulators. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the console is a 32-bit **MIPS R3000A** processor clocked at roughly 33.8 MHz, complemented by a specialised geometry coprocessor, the **GTE**, for 3D transformation calculations. The graphics core could render on the order of hundreds of thousands of textured polygons per second and worked at resolutions from roughly 256×224 up to 640×480 pixels with a palette of up to 16.7 million colours. The PlayStation does, however, have an unmistakable visual „signature“ that is enjoying a nostalgic renaissance today. The console was unable to **perspective-correct textures** or calculate depth precisely with floating point — it rounded coordinates to whole numbers. The result is the characteristic „swimming“ and jitter of textures and polygons as the camera moves. The hardware also lacked a proper z-buffer, so fog and darkness were widely used to hide the draw distance. It is precisely this aesthetic that indie creators deliberately imitate today under the „PS1 style“ banner. Sound was handled by a dedicated **SPU** chip with **24 hardware channels**, support for ADPCM samples and hardware reverb. Thanks to this, games sounded rich and, besides synthesised music, could also play full **CD Audio** tracks straight from the disc. ### Connectivity and peripherals The standard was a **memory card** with a capacity of 128 kB (15 blocks), onto which saves were stored — an absolute necessity for large RPGs. The console had two controller ports and two card ports. The original controller had no sticks; the turning point was the **DualShock** (1997/1998) with two analog sticks and vibration, which foreshadowed today's standard. Among the peripherals were the **multitap** for connecting up to four (or eight) players, the **GunCon** light gun from Namco, a steering wheel, dance mats and, in Japan, even a modem and a mouse. A **Link Cable** existed for connecting two consoles (e.g. for splitting into two screens in racing games). Output went through a proprietary **multi-out** connector, which offered composite, S-Video and RGB SCART — RGB gave the sharpest picture. ### Models and revisions The original model bore the designation **SCPH-1000** and further numerical series. Gradual revisions cut manufacturing costs and addressed problems — the troubles with worn optics and skipping on older units were notorious, and could be alleviated by turning the console upside down. Later versions also removed the separate **parallel (parallel I/O)** port used by cheating devices, as well as the serial port. A major redesign came in 2000 with the **PS one** — a markedly smaller, rounded console intended for a new generation of buyers, for which a small LCD screen could also be bought to play away from the television. The console remained fully compatible with the original library. Its successor, the **PlayStation 2**, could moreover play the vast majority of PS1 games thanks to related hardware, thereby extending the titles' lifespan even further. ### Clones and variants Sony guarded the brand strictly, so legal „clones“ in the spirit of famiclones practically did not exist. In the post-Soviet and Eastern European space — the Czech Republic included — however, **piracy** became a phenomenon: thanks to modchips (small chips bypassing regional and copy protection) and burned CDs, the PlayStation spread here too in the 1990s and around the turn of the millennium, where original titles were financially out of reach for many. Marketplaces and flea markets with burned discs were a common reality back then. It was a grey-to-black scene, not official hardware clones. ### Today's scene PS1 emulation is among the most mature there is. On PC and handheld systems, **DuckStation** excels, while on weaker devices and within RetroArch the **PCSX-ReARMed** core serves well. Emulators moreover offer improvements no one dreamed of in the 1990s — higher internal resolution, perspective correction of textures (an end to the „swimming“), filtering and a widescreen hack. Sony itself released the miniature **PlayStation Classic** in 2018 with pre-installed games. For true enthusiasts, though, the most rewarding path remains emulation with one's own disc backups — just bear in mind that CD images take up considerably more space on an SD card than cartridge consoles. The library is so rich that the hardest question remains: where to begin.

psp.history: When Sony unveiled the PlayStation Portable in 2004 (in Japan on 12 December 2004, in Europe in the spring of 2005), it was the boldest assault on the portable market anyone had ever undertaken up to that point. Nintendo had held handheld gaming in its grip for more than fifteen years — from the Game Boy through the Game Boy Color to the Game Boy Advance. The PSP was the first console to promise a true **console experience in your pocket**: a widescreen display, smooth 3D graphics close to the PlayStation 2, and multimedia ambitions no one had crammed into a handheld gaming machine before. The Nintendo DS stood against the PSP with its two displays and touch. Both devices ultimately found an audience — the DS won in sales, but the PSP became a darling of players who wanted „big“ games on the go as well. And not just players: thanks to its openness to custom code, one of the liveliest homebrew and emulation scenes ever formed around it. ### Technology: graphics and sound At the heart of the PSP is a pair of processors based on the MIPS R4000 architecture — the main CPU and a separate **Media Engine**, both clocked variably up to 333 MHz (the original firmware limited them to 222 MHz for the sake of battery life). Graphics are handled by a custom GPU with 2 MB of video memory, and the system has a further 32 MB of main RAM (models from the PSP-2000 onward received double, i.e. 64 MB). The original model's display measures 4.3 inches and offers a resolution of **480 × 272 pixels** in 16:9 with 16.77 million colours — for the year 2005 it was an exceptionally sharp and colourful panel. The GPU handled hardware **texturing, gouraud shading and transformations**, thanks to which titles like God of War or GTA came visually close to their „big“ console counterparts. Sound is handled by a hardware decoder capable of formats such as ATRAC3 and MP3 and multichannel output; stereo speakers are complemented by a headphone output. For both music and games it was clean, quality sound — the PSP was, after all, also sold as a portable media player. ### Connectivity and peripherals The PSP had rich connectivity for its time. Built-in **Wi-Fi (802.11b)** enabled local multiplayer as well as internet connection — in Japan, an entire social culture of communal hunting formed around Monster Hunter thanks to it. Only the original PSP-1000 model had an infrared port. Media was loaded from a proprietary optical format, the **UMD (Universal Media Disc)** — small discs in a protective case with a capacity of around 1.8 GB. Alongside games, Sony also released films on them, though that turned out to be a dead end. Data and saves were stored on **Memory Stick PRO Duo** cards. The console offered AV output for connecting to a television (on the PSP-2000 model and newer, component and composite video as well). ### Models and revisions The Sony PSP went through several major redesigns: - **PSP-1000** (2004) — the original „fat“ model, robust, with an IR port and 32 MB of RAM. - **PSP-2000 „Slim & Lite“** (2007) — markedly thinner and lighter, 64 MB of RAM, faster loading from UMD, video output and the ability to charge via USB. - **PSP-3000** (2008) — an improved display with better colour rendition and reduced motion blur, a built-in microphone. - **PSP Go (PSP-N1000)** (2009) — a radical shift: a sliding design, **no UMD drive**, just 16 GB of internal memory and purely digital distribution via the PlayStation Store. It arrived too early, however, into a time without fast and ubiquitous internet, and failed commercially. - **PSP-E1000 „Street“** (2011) — a cheap model without Wi-Fi and with a mono speaker, intended for a budget deployment in Europe. ### Clones and variants Genuine hardware clones of the PSP practically did not exist — it was a closed, technically demanding system. Cheap Asian „PSP-like“ players imitating the design did appear, but they have nothing to do with its actual game library. The platform's true „extension“ became the **homebrew scene**: after the firmware was cracked (custom firmware such as M33 and later the Pro-CFW series), the PSP became a favourite tool of enthusiasts. Emulators of eight-bit and sixteen-bit systems ran on it, and a huge community of custom applications sprang up — which made the PSP a legend among tinkerers, albeit against Sony's will. ### Today's scene The PSP is very much alive among emulation enthusiasts today. The top of the line is **PPSSPP** — a mature, open-source emulator running on PC, Android, iOS and a whole range of handheld retro consoles, which can increase resolution, smooth textures and speed up loading beyond the original. For retro gaming on a handheld console, the PSP is a rewarding but more demanding platform. 2D and lighter 3D titles run superbly on H700-class chips, while the heaviest 3D games like God of War will appreciate more powerful hardware — the RG46R handles them noticeably better than the RG35XX Pro. The size of the games is moreover considerable compared to older systems, so a spacious memory card pays off. But whoever wants to carry truly „big“ games in their pocket will find a real treasure in the PSP library — from God of War through Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker to Patapon and LocoRoco.

n64.history: The Nintendo 64 hit the market in 1996 as a console full of contradictions. Technically it was in some respects ahead of the competition — it handled smooth 3D, perspective-correct texturing and hardware antialiasing, something neither the PlayStation nor the Saturn could attempt. But Nintendo made a fateful decision: to stick with cartridges at the very moment the rest of the industry moved to CDs. Cartridges ran without loading times and were hard to pirate, but they were expensive and limited in capacity. That put off many publishers, who left for Sony — the most famous example being Square, which, thanks to the space on a CD, moved **Final Fantasy VII** from the N64 to the PlayStation. Even so, the N64 brought innovations we still use today. Its controller was the first with an analog stick designed specifically for movement in 3D space — which only seemed obvious once **Super Mario 64** had demonstrated it to perfection. And it had four controller ports right in the body of the console, making the N64 the king of local four-player multiplayer: **GoldenEye 007**, **Mario Kart 64** and the Mario Party series defined an entire era of couch gaming. ### Technology: graphics and sound The heart of the console is the 64-bit **NEC VR4300** processor (a variant of the MIPS R4300i) clocked at 93.75 MHz and the **Reality Coprocessor (RCP)** from SGI at 62.5 MHz, which handles both geometry and rasterization. The console carries 4 MB of shared Rambus RDRAM memory, expandable to 8 MB via the Expansion Pak. The N64 handled perspective-correct texture mapping, a Z-buffer, fog and, above all, trilinear filtering and full-screen antialiasing. That is precisely what gives the N64 its characteristic "soft", almost hazy look — the opposite of the sharp but jittery textures of the PS1. You either love the blurry aesthetic or you don't, but it is unmistakable. The price for ambitious 3D was often a low frame rate and the small texture cache of the RCP (only around 4 KB), because of which textures in some games looked blurry and repetitive. Resolution ranged from roughly 320×240 up to 640×480 in high mode (typically with the Expansion Pak, e.g. in Perfect Dark). Sound was not handled by a separate chip in the classic sense — synthesis was done by the RCP in software, so audio quality depended on how much computing power developers allocated to it. This allowed high-quality streamed sequences and spatial sound, but it ate into the power available for graphics. ### Connectivity and peripherals A key peripheral was the **Rumble Pak** — a vibration module for the controller, popularized by **Star Fox 64** (Lylat Wars in Europe). The same slot on the back of the controller also accepted the **Controller Pak**, a memory card for saving game progress in games that did not have battery-backed memory in the cartridge. The **Expansion Pak** doubled the RAM to 8 MB and was mandatory for Donkey Kong 64 and the high mode of Perfect Dark. A special chapter is the **64DD** — a magneto-optical disk drive attached from below, which, however, was released only in Japan and flopped commercially. The N64 offered both composite and S-Video output; NTSC versions also supported RGB, whereas PAL units usually did not. ### Models and revisions Alongside the standard grey console came a range of colored variants and transparent editions (Funtastic Series, Jusco). Three main regional versions were sold around the world — NTSC-U, NTSC-J and PAL. In Japan there was a **Pikachu N64** with a built-in Pokémon design. The later redesign, the **iQue Player** (2003), was intended exclusively for the Chinese market: it was an N64 built directly into the controller, with games loaded onto a memory card. Related technology was also used by the betting arcade board **Aleck 64**. ### Clones and variants Official N64 clones practically did not exist — the cartridge architecture and Nintendo's guarded lockout complicated the manufacture of imitations, unlike with the NES. In Czechoslovakia and the Eastern Bloc, the N64 (which arrived only after the Velvet Revolution) was therefore sold rather marginally and expensively; the 8-bit and 16-bit era here was defined by other machines — famiclones like the **Pegasus** for the NES or the domestic **Didaktik** as a ZX Spectrum clone.
