It was a single-chip solution combining CPU and GPU on the same silicon, complemented by **8 GB of GDDR5 memory** shared between the processor and the graphics. This unified memory eliminated the bottlenecks known from the previous generation and gave developers greater freedom.

Graphics performance amounted to roughly 1.84 teraflops, enough for a stable **1080p** in most titles. An architecture close to a regular PC fundamentally simplified porting games between platforms, a key advantage throughout the machine's entire life cycle.

### DualShock 4 and peripherals

The **DualShock 4** controller marked the most significant redesign in the history of the lineup since the original PlayStation. Its most striking novelty was the **touchpad** on the front, which developers used for everything from menu gestures to unconventional mechanics. Beneath it sat the **Share** button, allowing screenshots and videos to be shared to social networks with a single press.

The controller also gained a **light bar**, used to identify players as well as a gameplay element reacting to on-screen events, and combined with the **PlayStation Camera** it also enabled motion tracking. The camera and DualShock 4 formed the foundation for the **PlayStation VR** headset, which brought virtual reality into homes on a mainstream scale.

### PSN, online, and services

A major, if controversial, milestone was making online play a paid feature through **PlayStation Plus** — unlike the PS3, multiplayer online required a subscription. In return, subscribers received free monthly games, store discounts, and cloud storage.

The **PSN** network grew over the PS4's lifetime into one of the largest gaming platforms in the world, with features like streaming to Twitch/YouTube and gradually expanding cross-play. The **PlayStation Now** service offered streaming of older games without the need to download them, foreshadowing the direction the gaming industry would start to take.

### Models and revisions (Slim, PS4 Pro)

The original PS4 model was slimmed down in 2016 into the **PS4 Slim** — a smaller, more energy-efficient case with the same performance. That same year, however, brought a far more important novelty: the **PlayStation 4 Pro**.

The PS4 Pro offered significantly boosted graphics (around 4.2 teraflops), enabling gameplay in **4K resolution** (often via checkerboard rendering) and support for **HDR**. It was the first example of a so-called mid-generation console — Sony did not force players to buy new hardware, only offering an upgrade for those who wanted better graphics, while games remained compatible across models. Microsoft later adopted the concept with the Xbox One X.

### Significance and legacy

The PlayStation 4 went down in history as the console that **corrected its predecessor's mistakes** and showed that developer-friendliness is valued more than exotic performance on paper. A strong lineup of exclusive titles, openness toward the indie scene, and a smart business strategy made it the winner of the eighth console generation. Today the PS4 is gradually passing into the hands of emulators and retro enthusiasts, but in significance it stands alongside the PlayStation 2 as one of the pillars of Sony's dominance in the home console market.

xbox-one.history:
When Microsoft unveiled the Xbox One in May 2013, a confident answer to the successful Xbox 360 was expected. Instead came one of the most unfortunate reveals in the history of the gaming industry. The company chose to present the console as a universal "all-in-one" living-room entertainment hub — emphasizing television, movies, and voice control via **Kinect** — while games briefly seemed like an afterthought. Rival Sony reacted cleverly: the PlayStation 4 offered a simpler, cheaper, and more player-friendly solution, kicking off one of the most decisive generational victories in console history.

Still, the Xbox One ultimately wasn't a flop — it merely lost the battle for first place. Microsoft managed a sharp course correction after a disastrous start, listened to the community, and gradually built the console into a platform that still defines today's Xbox Game Pass and the philosophy of services layered over hardware.

### A controversial start (DRM, Kinect)

Xbox One inflicted the biggest blow on itself, even before launch. Microsoft planned an **always-online DRM** system — the console was to connect to the internet at least once every 24 hours to verify licenses, and games could only be installed and resold under restrictions resembling digital distribution. On top of that came the requirement to have the **Kinect** sensor connected and switched on (it was included with every unit), which watched the living room via camera and microphone — sparking a wave of privacy concerns. A price of 499 dollars, a hundred dollars higher than the PS4, only underscored the whole package.

The reaction from players and journalists was so strong that Microsoft capitulated within a few weeks: in June 2013 it announced the cancellation of the always-online requirement, the removal of restrictions on sharing and reselling games, and made the Kinect detachable. The reputational damage, however, had already been done, and the Xbox One entered the generation with a lost head start it never fully made up.

### Technology: graphics and sound

Microsoft built the Xbox One around its own AMD APU with an **x86-64** architecture, containing eight **Jaguar** cores and a graphics core from the **Radeon** (GCN) family. It was the same philosophy as the PlayStation 4 — a unified, PC-like architecture that finally made it easier for developers to port games between platforms and to computers.

The difference lay in memory: while the PS4 bet on faster 8 GB of GDDR5 shared between CPU and GPU, the Xbox One used 8 GB of slower **DDR3** supplemented by 32 MB of fast **ESRAM** cache meant to compensate for the bandwidth shortfall. In practice, this meant the Xbox One had, proportionally, lower net graphics performance than the competition, and many multiplatform games ran on the PS4 at a higher resolution or higher frame rate — a gap that journalists and players tracked title after title throughout the entire generation.

### Xbox Live, backward compatibility, and Game Pass

Where the Xbox One lost on paper specs, it made up for it in services. **Xbox Live** remained the generation's most advanced online infrastructure, but the real turnaround came with **backward compatibility** — Microsoft gradually enabled playback of hundreds of games from the **Xbox 360** and even the original **Xbox**, making the Xbox One the only console able to play titles from three generations back. It was a technically demanding hardware-level emulation project that earned praise even from players who otherwise remained skeptical of Microsoft.

An even bigger impact came in 2017 with the launch of **Xbox Game Pass** — a subscription that, for a monthly fee, unlocked a growing library of downloadable games, including Microsoft's new releases on day one. This model, later expanded to PC and cloud, became the core of the company's entire strategy and is still regarded today as one of the most significant moves in modern console history.

### Models and revisions (S, One X)

The base Xbox One from November 2013 got a successor in 2016, the **Xbox One S** — smaller, quieter, without an external power brick, supporting **4K video and HDR** for movies and streaming, even though it still rendered games at a lower resolution.

The true technical peak of the generation was the **Xbox One X** of 2017, which Microsoft marketed as "the most powerful console in the world." It brought a significantly stronger GPU, 12 GB of GDDR5 memory, and the ability to render a number of games in genuine **4K resolution**, for the first time in the generation surpassing the PlayStation 4 Pro in raw hardware terms. It was a smaller but enthusiast-cherished machine that showed Microsoft had learned from the mistakes of 2013.

### Significance and legacy

The Xbox One ultimately sold roughly **50 million units** — noticeably fewer than the PlayStation 4's more than 117 million — and in console history remains a reminder of how costly a poorly handled product reveal can be. At the same time, it's also an example of a turnaround: a company that in 2013 nearly lost the trust of its own community laid, in the years that followed, the foundations for what Xbox is today — a platform built on subscriptions, backward compatibility, and cross-device availability rather than the raw power of a single piece of hardware. The Game Pass and cross-generation gaming philosophy that the Xbox One generation kicked off leads directly to today's Xbox Series X/S and defines how Microsoft positions itself in the console market to this day.

switch.history:
When Nintendo launched the Switch in March 2017, it bet on a concept that no one had ever fully pulled off before: a console that is both a home system hooked up to the TV and a full-fledged handheld in your pocket. After the commercial flop of the Wii U, it was a huge gamble — and it paid off completely. The Switch launched alongside **The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild**, a title that instantly showed what the hybrid design could do and became one of the most acclaimed games of all time. Within a few years, the Switch became one of the most successful consoles in gaming history, with sales exceeding 140 million units.

### Hybrid concept (dock, handheld, tabletop)

The foundation of the whole success was a simple yet brilliant idea: one device, three ways to play. In **docked mode**, the tablet slots into a dock connected to the television, and both the picture and performance scale up for the big screen. Pull it out of the dock and the game transitions without interruption to the built-in display, turning the Switch into a classic **handheld**. The third option is **tabletop mode** — the console stands on its own flip-out kickstand, the controllers detach, and two people can play directly off the display without a TV. It was this flexibility, not raw power, that defined the entire generation.

### Technology: graphics and sound

At the heart of the Switch is the **NVIDIA Tegra X1** chip with an **ARM** architecture (a quad-core ARM Cortex-A57 CPU and graphics based on the Maxwell architecture), paired with 4 GB of RAM. Performance scales dynamically depending on the mode — docked, the chip runs at a higher clock and games typically target 900p to 1080p, while in portable mode the clock drops to save battery and resolution falls to match the 720p display. This scalability made it possible to bring even graphically demanding titles like **The Witcher 3** or **DOOM** to the system, though often at the cost of compromises in frame rate and detail.

Audio is handled through standard stereo speakers built into the console body, with output via a 3.5mm jack or HDMI when docked. Built-in storage (32 GB on the base model, later 64 GB) is supplemented by a microSD card slot, since games are distributed both physically on **cartridges** and digitally through the eShop.

### Joy-Cons and peripherals

The Switch's most distinctive feature is its detachable **Joy-Con** controllers, which clip onto the sides of the tablet via rails, or can be separated to function as a pair of independent mini controllers — ideal for spontaneous multiplayer without any extra hardware. Each Joy-Con includes **HD rumble** (finely graded vibration feedback capable of simulating things like dice rattling in a cup) and **motion sensors** used in games like 1-2-Switch or Mario Kart 8 Deluxe. The right Joy-Con additionally carries an infrared camera. For television play there's the classic **Pro Controller**. Nintendo also built an experimental peripheral line around the hardware called **Nintendo Labo** — cardboard construction kits that the Joy-Cons slot into, turning the console into a fishing rod, a robot, or a motorbike using infrared sensing and vibration.

### Models and revisions (Lite, OLED)

The original model stayed on sale unchanged for several years, later receiving only quieter cooling and a slightly longer battery life. In 2019 came the **Nintendo Switch Lite** — a lightened, purely handheld version with no docking capability and fixed-in-place controllers, aimed at players who don't use TV mode. Then in 2021 came the **OLED model**: a larger 7-inch screen with richer colors and deeper blacks, an improved kickstand, and steadier battery life, while the chip's raw performance stayed unchanged. All three variants are mutually compatible with the same game library and peripherals.

### Significance and legacy

The Switch conclusively proved that the hybrid approach isn't a compromise but a full-fledged design philosophy — a console that goes anywhere with the player while still offering an experience comparable to sitting in front of the TV. The combination of a strong lineup of exclusives, the social potential of the Joy-Cons, and clever performance scalability made it one of the best-selling platforms of all time and a blueprint that other portable and hybrid systems are now modeled after.

ps-vita.history:
When Sony unveiled the PlayStation Vita on December 17, 2011 in Japan (and in February 2012 in western markets), it looked like a dream come true for anyone who'd ever complained about the PSP's missing second stick. The Vita was an almost absurdly well-built piece of hardware: a gorgeous OLED display, a quad-core processor, and touch controls on both the front and back. It was also **Sony's last major attempt at a classic handheld** — and although it's technically one of the best-designed pocket machines in history, commercially it fell flat.

There were several reasons. Standing directly against the Vita was **Nintendo's 3DS**, with cheaper hardware, stronger brands, and a year's head start. But a far bigger enemy that nobody had counted on was **smartphones**. By 2012, almost everyone already had a device in their pocket that could run games for free or for pocket change, and the market for expensive dedicated handhelds began to collapse. On top of that, Sony largely stopped supporting the Vita with its own big-name titles after a few years and let it survive on Japanese games and the indie scene.

And yet — or perhaps precisely because of that — the Vita has earned a cult reputation today. Whoever bought one back then rarely regretted it.

### Hardware: graphics and sound

At the Vita's heart sits a **quad-core ARM Cortex-A9**, paired with **PowerVR SGX543MP4+** graphics — the same quad-core variant of the chip that powered top-end tablets at the time. The system has **512 MB of RAM plus another 128 MB of VRAM**, which in 2012 made it the most powerful handheld gaming machine on the market by a wide margin.

The pride of the original model is its **5" OLED display at 960 × 544 pixels**, exactly four times the resolution of the PSP. The combination of absolute black and saturated colors was genuinely shocking at the time and still ranks among the most beautiful things you can look at on a handheld console today. The later PCH-2000 model switched to LCD, which is the one thing fans have never forgiven it for.

Control-wise, the console was revolutionary above all thanks to its **two analog sticks** — the first time in the history of a Sony handheld. Alongside them, the Vita offers a **front touchscreen as well as a rear touchpad**, a gyroscope with accelerometer, and **two cameras**. The rear touchpad, however, was an idea developers never quite figured out what to do with — it ended up used more as a curiosity than as a fully-fledged input method.

Audio is handled by stereo speakers and a quality headphone output; even with basic headphones, the Vita sounds clean and loud.

### Connectivity and peripherals

Games shipped on **proprietary PS Vita cards** — small flash media that replaced the PSP's optical UMDs. Alongside them, full **digital distribution through the PlayStation Store** eventually became home to the vast majority of the indie catalog.

The platform's biggest pain point was **Sony's memory cards**. The Vita refused to work with ordinary microSD cards and demanded its own proprietary format, priced absurdly — a 32GB card could easily cost as much as half the console itself. A textbook example of a decision that hurt the platform more than any competitor did.

Connectivity itself, on the other hand, was strong: **Wi-Fi** on all models, and **3G** on select versions. **Remote Play** worked beautifully — streaming games from the PlayStation 3 and, above all, from the PlayStation 4, where the Vita served as a second screen for the whole household. Sony also added **cross-buy** (buy a game once, play it on both PS4 and Vita) along with cross-play and cross-save between the platforms.

### Models and revisions

The PS Vita family stayed fairly compact:

- **PCH-1000** (2011) — the original model with a **5" OLED display**, available in Wi-Fi and 3G versions. Heavier, but with the best picture.
- **PCH-2000 "Slim"** (2013) — a thinner and noticeably lighter revision with an **LCD display** instead of OLED, longer battery life, 1 GB of internal storage, and microUSB charging. More practical, but a visual step backward.
- **PlayStation TV (Vita TV)** (2013) — a small **set-top box** built on Vita hardware that displayed games on a television and was controlled with a DualShock. Due to limited compatibility (titles relying on touch and gyroscope controls fell away), it was more of an interesting experiment than anything else.

### Clones and variants

No classic clones of the Vita ever appeared — the hardware was closed and complicated to replicate. Its legacy lies elsewhere: the Vita was **the first console to convincingly prove that full-fledged games belong in your pocket**, and it's exactly that idea that the wave of handheld gaming PCs would carry to completion a decade later. The **Steam Deck**, the ASUS ROG Ally, and other machines are essentially doing what the Vita did — just with a library no longer locked to a single manufacturer.

Sony returned to the idea in 2023 with the **PlayStation Portal**, though it isn't a standalone console at all: it's purely a streaming screen for the PS5. The irony is that the Vita could already do exactly that function a decade earlier — and it could also play its own games on top of it.

### The scene today

The Vita has one of the best **homebrew scenes** around, period. The breakthrough came with **HENkaku** and the tools that followed, which made it possible to run custom code on practically every firmware version. The result is a console that can be turned into an excellent emulation machine — handling everything from 8-bit systems through PS1 and GBA to a solid chunk of the PSP library — and one that also supports ordinary microSD cards via an adapter that fits into the game card slot. That neatly sidesteps the original sin of the platform's expensive memory cards.

Production of the console ended in **2019**, and along with it went the ability to buy new titles from the store. Even so, the Vita doesn't feel like a dead platform. Its catalog — packed with **JRPGs** (Persona 4 Golden, Danganronpa, Ys, Trails), superb ports, and indie gems like Hotline Miami or Spelunky — remains a very good reason to pick one up today. And whoever holds an original OLED model in their hands will understand within seconds why it's called the most beautiful handheld console ever made.
